adversarial_test_results.prompt:
The expedition had begun in the spring, when the river was still swollen with meltwater from the northern ranges. Four researchers, two guides and a cook travelled by boat to the abandoned survey station, a cluster of wooden buildings that had not been used for more than a decade. The first weeks were spent repairing the roof, clearing the trail and sorting the crates of instruments that had been shipped ahead of them. Mornings were cold, and the fog rarely lifted before noon.

Their plan was simple. Each day one team measured the depth of the channel at fixed intervals, while another recorded the temperature of the water and the speed of the current. The cook kept a ledger of supplies, and the guides marked the places where the bank had collapsed after the spring floods. In the evenings everyone gathered around the stove to compare notes and to argue about what the numbers meant.

By midsummer a pattern had become clear. The channel was widening, slowly but steadily, and the shallows downstream were filling with sand. The oldest guide, who had worked on the river for thirty years, said that he had seen the same thing once before, in a season when the winter snows had been unusually heavy. Nobody had written it down at the time, so the observation could not be checked.

The team decided to extend the survey through the autumn. More instruments were ordered, and a second boat was brought up from the depot. Supplies arrived once a month, carried up from the village by mule, and the cook counted every tin twice. The work became routine: measure, record, return, argue, sleep. Rain interrupted them for days at a time, and on those days they read the old reports in the station library and copied long passages into their notebooks.

In the final week they packed the equipment, labelled the samples and wrote a short report for the ministry. The report described the measurements, the weather, the condition of the banks and the state of the buildings. It ended with a single recommendation, phrased as carefully as they could manage: that the monitoring programme should continue, and that the data should be published so that other teams could compare their results with ours.

On the last morning the fog lifted early and the river lay flat and bright below the ridge. They loaded the boats, checked the fuel and waited for the cook, who was still washing the last of the pans. When she finally came down to the landing she was carrying a box of samples that everyone had forgotten, and the guide laughed and said that this was exactly how the previous expedition had lost its
most valuable crate.
